summary.text: The continued-fraction recurrence yields \(a(n)=P(n)/\gcd(P(n),2(n-1)(n-3)!)\), where \(P(n)=n^2+2n-4\). Quadratic reciprocity makes \(5\) a square modulo \(p\), so choosing \(n+1\) to be a square root gives \(P(n)=pm\); a short analysis of the five residues immediately below \(p\) shows (apart from explicitly handled small cases) that \(p\ge n+6\), hence \(m<n-2\) and \(m\mid(n-3)!\), while \(p\) is coprime to the other gcd argument, so the gcd is exactly \(m\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
P(n)=n^2+2n-4.
\]
We first derive a formula for the reduced denominator in the sequence, and then use that formula to construct an index for every prime in the required congruence classes.

For a fixed integer \(n\ge 3\), define the successive inner denominators of the continued fraction by
\[
R_{n-1}=(n-1)+\frac n4
\]
and, descending from \(k=n-2\) to \(k=2\), by
\[
R_k=k-\frac{k+1}{R_{k+1}}.
\]
Thus the continued fraction in the statement is \(1/R_2\). If \(R_2=N/D\) in lowest terms, then \(1/R_2=D/N\), so the sequence value \(a(n)\) is \(|N|\), the absolute value of the reduced numerator of \(R_2\).

We now express \(R_2\) by integer continuants. For fixed \(n\), define integers \(q_k\) by
\[
q_{n+1}=-1,\qquad q_n=4,
\]
and, for \(k<n\),
\[
q_k=kq_{k+1}-(k+1)q_{k+2}.
\]
At the first step this gives
\[
q_{n-1}=(n-1)q_n-nq_{n+1}=4(n-1)+n=5n-4.
\]
Consequently
\[
\frac{q_{n-1}}{q_n}=\frac{5n-4}{4}=(n-1)+\frac n4=R_{n-1}.
\]
Moreover, whenever \(R_{k+1}=q_{k+1}/q_{k+2}\), the defining recurrence gives
\[
R_k=k-\frac{k+1}{R_{k+1}}
   =k-(k+1)\frac{q_{k+2}}{q_{k+1}}
   =\frac{kq_{k+1}-(k+1)q_{k+2}}{q_{k+1}}
   =\frac{q_k}{q_{k+1}}.
\]
Hence, by descending induction,
\[
R_k=\frac{q_k}{q_{k+1}},
\qquad	ext{in particular}\qquad
R_2=\frac{q_2}{q_3}.
\]
The identities below also show that the relevant intermediate denominators are nonzero, so these rational expressions are well-defined.

We need explicit information about \(q_2\) and \(q_3\). For \(t\ge 0\), put
\[
S_t=\sum_{i=0}^{t-1}i!,
\]
with \(S_0=0\). For \(3\le k\le n+1\), set
\[
h_k=(k-1)(k-3)!\,q_k.
\]
We claim that
\[
 h_k=4(n-1)(n-3)!+P(n)\bigl(S_{n-3}-S_{k-3}\bigr). \tag{1}
\]
Here and below these are integer identities; at \(k=n+1\), the factorial notation in the left side gives
\(h_{n+1}=n(n-2)!q_{n+1}=-n(n-2)!\).

To prove (1), first observe that the recurrence for the \(q_k\)'s implies, for \(3\le k<n\),
\[
(k-2)h_k=(k-1)h_{k+1}-h_{k+2}. \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, multiplying
\(q_k=kq_{k+1}-(k+1)q_{k+2}\)
by \((k-2)(k-1)(k-3)!\), and using
\((k-2)!=(k-2)(k-3)!\) and
\((k-1)!=(k-1)(k-2)(k-3)!\), gives exactly (2).

The right side of (1), regarded as a function of \(k\), satisfies the same recurrence. This follows from
\[
S_{k-2}=S_{k-3}+(k-3)!,
\qquad
S_{k-1}=S_{k-3}+(k-3)!+(k-2)!,
\]
together with \((k-2)!=(k-2)(k-3)!\). Substitution into (2) makes the constant term and the coefficient of \(P(n)\) agree separately.

It remains to check two terminal values. At \(k=n\), since \(q_n=4\),
\[
h_n=4(n-1)(n-3)!,
\]
which agrees with (1), because \(S_{n-3}-S_{n-3}=0\). At \(k=n+1\), the left side is
\[
h_{n+1}=-n(n-2)!.
\]
On the proposed right side, \(S_{n-2}=S_{n-3}+(n-3)!\), so its value is
\[
4(n-1)(n-3)!-P(n)(n-3)!
 =\bigl(4(n-1)-(n^2+2n-4)\bigr)(n-3)!.
\]
Since
\[
4(n-1)-(n^2+2n-4)=-n(n-2),
\]
this is \(-n(n-2)!\), as required. The common recurrence and these two terminal values prove (1) by descending induction.

We can now evaluate \(q_2\). The recurrence at \(k=2\) says
\[
q_2=2q_3-3q_4.
\]
But \(h_3=2q_3\) and \(h_4=3q_4\), so
\[
q_2=h_3-h_4.
\]
By (1), the constant terms cancel and
\[
q_2=P(n)\bigl(S_1-S_0\bigr)=P(n),
\]
because \(S_1=0!=1\) and \(S_0=0\). Thus
\[
q_2=n^2+2n-4. \tag{3}
\]

At \(k=3\), formula (1) gives
\[
2q_3=4(n-1)(n-3)!+P(n)S_{n-3}. \tag{4}
\]
If \(n\ge5\), then \(S_{n-3}\) is even: its first two terms are
\(0!+1!=2\), and every subsequent factorial \(i!\), for \(i\ge2\), is even. Therefore (4) yields the integer formula
\[
q_3=2(n-1)(n-3)!+P(n)\frac{S_{n-3}}2. \tag{5}
\]
In particular, since adding a multiple of the first gcd argument to the second does not change a gcd, (5) implies
\[
\gcd(P(n),q_3)
 =\gcd\bigl(P(n),\,2(n-1)(n-3)!\bigr). \tag{6}
\]
Also, the closed form (1) shows that the relevant \(q_k\)'s do not vanish for \(n\ge5\): for \(3\le k\le n\), both the leading term \(4(n-1)(n-3)!\) and the term involving \(P(n)>0\) and \(S_{n-3}-S_{k-3}\ge0\) are nonnegative, with the leading term positive, while \(q_{n+1}=-1\).

Since \(P(n)>0\) for \(n\ge2\), equations (3) and (6), together with \(R_2=q_2/q_3\), show that for every \(n\ge5\),
\[
a(n)=
\frac{P(n)}{\gcd\bigl(P(n),\,2(n-1)(n-3)!\bigr)}. \tag{7}
\]
Indeed, reducing the rational number \(P(n)/q_3\) divides its numerator by \(\gcd(P(n),q_3)\), and that reduced numerator is precisely the denominator of its reciprocal.

We now turn to the prime construction. Let \(p\) be prime and suppose
\[
p\equiv1\pmod {10}\qquad\text{or}\qquad p\equiv9\pmod {10}.
\]
Such a prime satisfies \(p\ge11\). In fact, in the first congruence class the only smaller nonnegative possibility is \(1\), which is not prime, while in the second class the only smaller possibility is \(9\), which is not prime.

We claim that \(5\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\). The congruence assumption gives
\[
p\equiv1\pmod5\qquad\text{or}\qquad p\equiv4\pmod5.
\]
Both residues are squares modulo \(5\): \(1\equiv1^2\pmod5\) and \(4\equiv2^2\pmod5\). Since \(p\ne2,5\), quadratic reciprocity applies. Because \(5\equiv1\pmod4\), its reciprocity sign is positive, and hence
\[
\left(\frac5p\right)=\left(\frac p5\right)=1.
\]
Therefore there is a residue \(r\pmod p\) such that
\[
r^2\equiv5\pmod p. \tag{8}
\]

Choose \(n\) to be the least nonnegative residue of \(r-1\) modulo \(p\). Thus
\[
0\le n<p,
\qquad n+1\equiv r\pmod p.
\]
By (8),
\[
(n+1)^2\equiv5\pmod p,
\]
and therefore
\[
P(n)=n^2+2n-4=(n+1)^2-5\equiv0\pmod p. \tag{9}
\]
Thus \(p\mid P(n)\).

We first dispose of the small possible values of \(n\). We must have \(n\ge3\). For \(n=0,1,2\), the values of \(P(n)\) are respectively \(-4,-1,4\), all nonzero and of absolute value less than \(p\). None can be divisible by \(p\ge11\), contradicting (9).

If \(n=3\), then \(P(3)=11\). Since \(p\ge11\) is prime and divides \(11\), necessarily \(p=11\). Directly evaluating the continued fraction at \(n=3\) gives
\[
\frac1{2-3/(-4)}=\frac1{2+3/4}=\frac4{11},
\]
so \(a(3)=11=p\), and we are done in this case.

The value \(n=4\) cannot occur: here \(P(4)=20\), and no prime \(p\ge11\) divides \(20\). We may therefore assume from now on that
\[
5\le n<p. \tag{10}
\]

Write
\[
P=P(n)=pm,
\]
where \(m=P/p\) is a positive integer. Put
\[
B=2(n-1)(n-3)!.
\]
We will prove
\[
\gcd(P,B)=m. \tag{11}
\]
This will immediately finish the proof via (7).

First, \(p\) and \(B\) are coprime. Indeed, \(p\) is an odd prime, so it does not divide \(2\). Since \(n<p\), it does not divide the positive number \(n-1<p\). Finally, it cannot divide \((n-3)!\), because every prime divisor of \((n-3)!\) is at most \(n-3<p\). By Euclid's lemma applied to the factors of \(B\), this proves
\[
\gcd(p,B)=1. \tag{12}
\]

Next we prove that
\[
m\mid B. \tag{13}
\]
There is one exceptional pair to handle directly. If \((n,p)=(6,11)\), then
\[
P(6)=36+12-4=44=11\cdot4,
\]
so \(m=4\). In this case
\[
B=2\cdot5\cdot3!=60,
\]
and indeed \(4\mid60\).

Assume now that \((n,p)\ne(6,11)\). We claim that
\[
p\ge n+6. \tag{14}
\]
Since \(n<p\), if (14) failed, then \(p=n+k\) for one of
\(k=1,2,3,4,5\). Equivalently, \(n=p-k\). Reducing \(P(n)\) modulo \(p\) gives
\[
P(p-k)=(p-k)^2+2(p-k)-4
       \equiv k^2-2k-4\pmod p.
\]
For \(k=1,2,3,4,5\), these five values are respectively
\[
-5,\quad -4,\quad -1,\quad 4,\quad 11.
\]
But \(p\mid P(n)\). For the first four values, this is impossible because \(p\ge11\) cannot divide a nonzero integer of absolute value at most \(5\). For the last value, \(p\mid11\), so \(p=11\), and then \(n=p-5=6\), which is precisely the excluded exceptional pair. This proves (14).

For \(n\ge5\), we have the strict inequality
\[
P(n)< (n+6)(n-2), \tag{15}
\]
because
\[
(n+6)(n-2)-P(n)
=(n^2+4n-12)-(n^2+2n-4)
=2n-8>0.
\]
Combining (14) and (15),
\[
pm=P(n)<(n+6)(n-2)\le p(n-2).
\]
As \(p>0\), cancellation gives
\[
m<n-2,
\]
and hence, since \(m\) is an integer,
\[
1\le m\le n-3.
\]
Every positive integer at most \(n-3\) divides \((n-3)!\). Therefore
\[
m\mid(n-3)!\mid B,
\]
which proves (13) also in the nonexceptional case.

Finally, (11) follows from (12) and (13). To see this explicitly, write \(B=mc\). Then
\[
\gcd(P,B)=\gcd(pm,mc)=m\gcd(p,c).
\]
Since \(c\mid B\) and \(p\) is coprime to \(B\), we have \(\gcd(p,c)=1\). Thus \(\gcd(P,B)=m\), as claimed.

Applying the sequence formula (7) at this \(n\), we obtain
\[
a(n)=\frac{P(n)}{\gcd(P(n),B)}
     =\frac{pm}{m}
     =p.
\]
Together with the already treated case \(n=3\), this proves that every prime congruent to \(1\) or \(9\) modulo \(10\) occurs in A363347.
